Minesweeper in Excel

This week, we are going to stay out of Excel Hell by having a little fun. Excel MVP Tom Hinkle posted on LinkedIn about how he created the classic Microsoft Windows game Minesweeper. Business Partner's Corner

​

Simplify, Simplify, Simplify.

​

As my partner Paul Barnhurst says, “Complex is easy, simple is hard.” or as Steve Jobs used to say, “Simple can be harder than complex.”

​

One of my mentors, Dino Bianco (who is the CEO of Kruger Products) has a phenomenal way of simplifying the P&L. Instead of making it an overly complex discussion, he simplifies the P&L into three buckets:

​

1) Topline – How is volume or revenue doing versus prior year and budget/forecast.

​

2) Margin % - This is an important metric as businesses in general should strive to keep % margin flat or increasing. Paying close attention to margin % is important.

​

3) Expenses – Marketing and selling, general and admin (sg&a) expenses would fall into this bucket. How are expenses tracking.

​

Dino is a CPA and grew up in the Finance world, before moving to Marketing, Sales, and now the CEO role. He has a tremendous vantage point that can help all of us.

​

This approach helps him, and the organization understand the financial picture very quickly and then helps them dive deeper into areas that need special attention.

​

For example, if the topline was down, he could call a meeting with the Sales team to put an urgent plan into action. Alternatively, if margin % was down, it would be important to understand what would get margins back on track.

​

As a Finance professional, it is important to ‘roll around in the data’ and understand the financial picture. From there it is an important skill set to effectively simplify for our stakeholders.

​

This helps us get to quick understanding and more importantly take ACTION, capitalize on opportunities, and avert threats.

The FP&A Guy's Tech Tips

​

Continuous Process Improvement. We often look to technology to solve our problems, but we should first focus on creating a culture of continuously improving our processes.

​

When optimizing processes, I like to use the 7-step framework that can be seen in the below image.

​

​

  1. Map the process - Start by mapping out the existing process. This ensures you understand all the steps and flows with the existing process.
  2. Analyze the process - Spend time analyzing each step of the process. Talk to people who own the different steps today and ask them what could be improved with the existing process.
  3. Redesign the workflow - Write down what the new process should look like and then diagram the new process workflow.
  4. Assign resources - Assign the correct resources to work on the process. Sometimes, this can be done by just one person but sometimes it will require multiple people to work on the project.
  5. Develop an implementation plan - Create a plan including timelines and milestones for implementing the new process.
  6. Execute the plan - Take the steps necessary to implement the new process.
  7. Monitor and Optimize - Once the new process is in place, make sure you take time to monitor the process and make changes as necessary to ensure it is an optimized process.

Ron's Recommendations

Grit by Angela Duckworth

​

One of my favourite books all time!

​

Duckworth explores the vital role of passion and perseverance in achieving long-term success, a concept that is universally applicable in Finance. Duckworth's research dismantles the myth that talent alone leads to success. Instead, she presents grit which is a unique blend of persistence and passion as the true driver behind extraordinary achievements.

​

For finance professionals, the implications of Duckworth's findings are profound. Our industry is characterized by its fast pace, high stakes, and frequent fluctuations, making resilience and determination essential traits for those who wish to excel. Duckworth shows through a series of compelling examples that grit can be cultivated, regardless of an individual's background or current level of expertise.

​

Key Takeaways for Finance Professionals:

​

Grit Over Talent: In Finance, where quantitative skill and sharp analytical abilities are highly valued, Duckworth’s research is a reminder that these talents are just the starting point. The capacity to persevere is what differentiates the exceptional from the average.

​

Passion as a Foundation: Duckworth argues that passion is not merely a fleeting interest but a deep, enduring fascination with the subject matter. For finance professionals, finding and nurturing a genuine interest in all elements of the business (well beyond Finance) can fuel long-term motivation and dedication.

​

Perseverance Through Challenges: Finance is fraught with challenges, and we are often the conscience of the organization. From inflationary times to economic recessions to investment decisions. Duckworth’s concept of grit encourages professionals to view setbacks not as failures but as essential steps in the journey towards mastery and success.

​

Building Grit: Duckworth provides actionable strategies for cultivating grit, such as setting long-term goals, embracing a practice-focused approach to skill development, and seeking purpose in work. For finance professionals, this might mean setting career milestones, engaging in deliberate practice to hone their skills, and aligning their financial expertise with broader societal or personal values.

​

The Role of Culture: Lastly, Duckworth emphasizes the significance of culture in fostering grit. For finance organizations, this underscores the importance of creating environments that encourage perseverance, celebrate resilience, and support continuous learning and improvement.

​

Conclusion:

​

"Grit" by Angela Duckworth offers invaluable insights for finance professionals seeking to thrive in their careers. By emphasizing the importance of passion and perseverance over innate talent, Duckworth provides a blueprint for achieving lasting success in the competitive and complex field of finance.
